You are a medical radiology simplification assistant. Convert the following diagnostic radiology imaging report into simple, plain English that the patient and their family can clearly understand (at a 6th-grade reading level).

=== EXTRACTED CLINICAL ENTITIES — YOU MUST RETAIN ALL OF THESE ===
Exam: Cranial MRI of Brain
  Sequences: T1-weighted, FLAIR, T2-weighted, SWI, DWI
  Contrast: no
  Clinical indication: Dizziness
Normal structures (reassure about these):
  ✓ Brainstem
  ✓ Cerebellum
  ✓ Fourth ventricle
  ✓ Posterior fossa cisterns
  ✓ Bilateral basal ganglia
  ✓ Internal capsules
  ✓ Corpus callosum
  ✓ Cerebral white and gray matter (excluding left parietal perivascular spaces)
  ✓ Third and lateral ventricles
  ✓ Sulci
  ✓ Major cerebral vascular structures
  ✓ Paranasal sinuses
  ✓ Middle ear aeration
  ✓ Nasopharynx
  ✓ Orbits
  ✓ Visualized bones
Incidental findings:
  • Physiologic cystic perivascular enlargement in the left parietal region
Radiologist impression: Cranial MRI findings within normal limits.
=================================================================
CRITICAL RETENTION RULE: Every entity, value, measurement, date, medication name, finding, and recommendation listed above MUST appear in your simplified output. Do not omit any of them.

Rules:
1. Explain the type of imaging scan conducted in simple words (e.g. 'cranial MRI (a detailed brain scan using magnetic fields and radio waves, without any radiation)').
2. Keep essential anatomical and medical terms but immediately explain each in parentheses on first use, e.g. 'cerebellum (the part of the brain that controls balance and coordination)'.
3. Clearly state what was found to be NORMAL first, providing reassurance about unaffected areas.
4. For any ABNORMAL findings (such as lesions, abscesses, ischemia, inflammation, or fractures):
   - Explain what the finding means in plain words without causing unnecessary panic.
   - Explain common terms simply: e.g. 'ischemic-gliotic lesions (tiny microscopic scar spots in the brain caused by reduced blood flow in the past, often seen with aging or high BP)'.
   - Clarify whether the finding is new, chronic, or requires further evaluation.
5. If the radiologist recommends further tests (e.g. follow-up CT, contrast scan, or consultation), state this clearly.
6. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs without bullet points or headers.
7. Preserve all factual observations; never guess, infer, or fabricate findings not in the report.
8. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
9. CRITICAL — ENTITY RETENTION: Every entity listed in the extracted entities block above MUST appear in your simplified output — including the scan modality and sequences, every normal structure listed, every abnormal finding with its location and severity, all measurements with units, the radiologist's overall impression, and every recommended follow-up action. Do not omit any of them.

Clinical: Dizziness.
Technique: Three-plane T1-weighted, FLAIR; axial T2-weighted, SWI, and DWI.
Findings:
The brainstem and cerebellum, fourth ventricle, and posterior fossa cisterns are normal.
The bilateral basal ganglia, internal capsules, and corpus callosum are normal.
Except for physiologic cystic perivascular enlargement in the left parietal region, the cerebral white and gray matter is normal.
No abnormality is noted on DWI and SWI images.
The third and lateral ventricles and sulci are normal.
The major cerebral vascular structures are patent and normal.
The paranasal sinuses and middle ear aeration, nasopharynx, and orbits are normal.
No abnormality is noted in the visualized bones.
Impression:
•	Cranial MRI findings within normal limits.

output_text:
You had a cranial MRI (a detailed brain scan using magnetic fields and radio waves, without any radiation) to help investigate your dizziness. The scan used several specific types of images, including T1-weighted, FLAIR, T2-weighted, SWI, and DWI sequences, and it was performed without using any contrast dye. The good news is that the radiologist’s overall impression is that the cranial MRI findings are within normal limits.

Most of the important parts of your head and brain look healthy. The brainstem (the part of the brain that connects to the spinal cord and controls basic life functions) and the cerebellum (the part of the brain that controls balance and coordination) are normal. The fourth ventricle (a fluid-filled space in the brain) and the posterior fossa cisterns (small fluid-filled spaces at the back of the brain) are also normal. The bilateral basal ganglia (deep brain structures involved in movement), the internal capsules (nerve pathways in the brain), and the corpus callosum (the bridge connecting the two halves of the brain) are all normal. The third and lateral ventricles (fluid-filled spaces in the center of the brain) and the sulci (the grooves on the surface of the brain) are normal. The major cerebral vascular structures (the main blood vessels in the brain) are open and normal. The paranasal sinuses (air-filled spaces around the nose and eyes), middle ear aeration (air in the middle ear), nasopharynx (the upper part of the throat behind the nose), and orbits (the eye sockets) are all normal. There are no abnormalities in the visualized bones.

There is one small, non-serious finding: physiologic cystic perivascular enlargement in the left parietal region. This means there are tiny, fluid-filled spaces around blood vessels in the left parietal lobe (the part of the brain involved in sensation and spatial awareness). This is considered a normal, age-related change and is not a sign of disease or damage. Except for this minor, normal variation, the cerebral white and gray matter (the different types of brain tissue) is normal. The DWI and SWI images, which look for specific types of tissue changes or bleeding, showed no abnormalities. No further tests or follow-up actions are recommended based on this report.
